examples.text: An efficient bureaucracy helped the European monarchs maintain better control over their states.
Trying to get a new library card felt like battling a giant bureaucracy of forms and signatures.

hard.real_world_analogy: The process of getting a passport; you have to visit different windows, fill out endless forms, and wait for many people to check them.

words.meaning: Full of energy, new ideas, and activity.

medium.simple_explanation: Characterized by constant change, activity, or progress.
medium.funny_explanation: Imagine a person who can't sit still and is always doing three things at once—that's dynamic.

examples.text: A dynamic economy was seen as a way to strengthen state power.
The dynamic duo finished the puzzle in record time because they worked so fast.

words.meaning: Old system where lords controlled land and people.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Refers to the old medieval social system that was being abolished to modernize states.
hard.simple_explanation: A medieval social system where people worked and fought for nobles who gave them protection and the use of land in return.
hard.funny_explanation: A deal where the landlord says: 'You can live on my dirt, but you have to fight my battles and give me half your carrots.'

examples.text: The abolition of feudalism was a major step towards creating a modern state power.
In the world of feudalism, you didn't have a job; you just had a lord who told you which cow to wash.

hard.real_world_analogy: Like renting an apartment where instead of paying money, you have to act as the landlord's personal bodyguard and gardener.

words.meaning: System where peasants were forced to work land.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Used to describe the low status of peasants who were legally bound to their lord's land.
hard.simple_explanation: The state of being a serf (a laborer bound to the land and subject to a landlord).
hard.funny_explanation: Being stuck to a farm like a piece of old chewing gum stuck to the bottom of a shoe.

examples.text: Ending serfdom allowed peasants to move freely and seek work in cities.
Serfdom is like being in a video game where you're not allowed to leave the starting village until the level boss says so.

hard.real_world_analogy: A subscription service you can never cancel, and you have to keep working for the company forever just to have a place to sit.

words.meaning: Ruling with total power and no shared control.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Describes the type of monarchies in Europe that held absolute power and didn't like dissent.
hard.simple_explanation: Relating to a ruler who has absolute power and does not take others' opinions into account.
hard.funny_explanation: The 'Because I said so!' style of leadership where nobody else gets a turn with the remote control.

examples.text: Autocratic monarchies in Europe were strengthened by modern administrative changes.
The toddler was quite autocratic; if he didn't get his blue bowl, nobody got to eat breakfast.

hard.real_world_analogy: A game where one person makes up all the rules as they go, and if you complain, you're immediately 'out'.

words.meaning: People chosen to act or speak for others.

medium.simple_explanation: People chosen to act or speak on behalf of others.
medium.funny_explanation: The kids you send to the principal's office to argue for a longer recess because they are the best talkers.

examples.text: Representatives of the major European powers met in Vienna.
Our class representatives are currently negotiating for better snacks in the vending machine.

words.meaning: An official agreement that ends a problem.

medium.simple_explanation: An official agreement intended to resolve a dispute or decide a situation.
medium.funny_explanation: The final 'peace treaty' you make with your sibling after a week of fighting over the TV remote.

examples.text: The powers met at Vienna to draw up a settlement for Europe.
We reached a settlement: I do the dishes, and he stops eating my hidden chocolate.

words.meaning: A high leader in some European governments.

medium.simple_explanation: A high-ranking government official, often the head of the government in some countries.
medium.funny_explanation: A very fancy title for the person who is basically the CEO of a country.

examples.text: The Congress of Vienna was hosted by the Austrian Chancellor, Duke Metternich.
If I were Chancellor, my first law would be that weekends must last three days.

words.meaning: People sent to represent others at meetings.

medium.simple_explanation: People sent to represent others at a conference or meeting.
medium.funny_explanation: The official 'away team' sent to a meeting to make sure their side gets what it wants.

examples.text: The delegates at the Congress discussed how to reorganize Europe.
The delegates from the Chess Club went to the meeting to demand more fancy hats.

words.meaning: To build or create something strong.

medium.simple_explanation: To create something strong and enduring through effort.
medium.funny_explanation: Like a blacksmith hammering hot metal into a sword, but instead of metal, you're using words and laws.

examples.text: Economists talked of how economic measures could help forge the nation together.
The two friends decided to forge a secret club dedicated to eating pizza.

words.meaning: In a way that relates to physical wealth.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Friedrich List argued that the Zollverein would strengthen the nation 'materially' (economically/physically).
hard.simple_explanation: In a way that relates to physical things, money, or possessions rather than the mind or spirit.
hard.funny_explanation: When you're not just 'rich in spirit,' but actually have a pile of shiny gold coins and a fridge full of snacks.

examples.text: The trade union would help the nation grow materially through increased productivity.
Winning the lottery didn't change his personality, but it definitely made him materially more comfortable!

hard.real_world_analogy: The difference between someone telling you 'Good Job!' (moral support) and giving you a $20 bill (material support).

words.meaning: How much work is done or goods made.

medium.simple_explanation: The rate at which goods are produced or work is completed.
medium.funny_explanation: How many levels of a game you can beat in an hour versus how long you spend staring at the start screen.

examples.text: The union was expected to stimulate internal productivity in Germany.
My productivity goes way up when there's a deadline and way down when there's a cat video.

words.meaning: Joining two or more things into one.

medium.simple_explanation: The process of joining two or more things together to form a single entity.
medium.funny_explanation: Like mixing different colors of playdough to get one giant blob of a new color.

examples.text: The aim was to raise national sentiment through a fusion of provincial interests.
The restaurant served a fusion of sushi and tacos, which sounds weird but tasted amazing.

words.meaning: Related to a specific province or local area.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Describes the local/regional interests that List wanted to fuse into a single national interest.
hard.simple_explanation: Relating to a small province or a local area, often implying a narrow or limited outlook.
hard.funny_explanation: Thinking that your tiny neighborhood is the entire universe and being shocked that other places have different types of bread.

examples.text: The goal was to merge individual and provincial interests into one national sentiment.
His provincial taste in food meant he refused to eat anything that wasn't grown in his own backyard.

hard.real_world_analogy: A sports fan who only cares about the local school team and has never even heard of the Olympics.

words.meaning: To cause a certain feeling or situation.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: List suggests that a free economic system would 'engender' (create or produce) national feeling.
hard.simple_explanation: To cause or give rise to a feeling, situation, or condition.
hard.funny_explanation: To plant a tiny seed of an idea and watch it explode into a giant sunflower of emotion.

examples.text: The economic success of the union helped engender a sense of pride among the people.
The principal's speech about a surprise holiday helped engender a lot of cheering in the hallway.

hard.real_world_analogy: Like when a catchy song starts playing and it slowly engenders a mood in the room where everyone starts tapping their feet.

words.meaning: Goals or purposes one wants to achieve.
Feeling of love and pride for one's country.

medium.simple_explanation: A strong feeling of pride and belonging to one's own country.
medium.funny_explanation: It's like being a super-fan of your country, wearing the flag as a cape and thinking your nation is the MVP of the world.

examples.text: Nationalism grew across Europe as people wanted their own independent nations.
His nationalism was so strong he tried to make the national anthem his phone's ringtone.

words.meaning: A formal written agreement between countries.

medium.simple_explanation: A formal written agreement between two or more countries.
medium.funny_explanation: A fancy, pinky-swear contract between countries, but with way more stamps and boring signatures.

examples.text: The Treaty of Vienna changed the map of Europe in 1815.
I tried to sign a treaty with my mom to end the war over cleaning my room.

words.meaning: The goal or purpose of an action.
Reversing or canceling a previous action.
Making things different from how they were.
A family that rules a country for generations.

medium.simple_explanation: A series of rulers who all belong to the same family.
medium.funny_explanation: A family business where the business is 'owning the country' and the inheritance is a crown instead of a used car.

examples.text: The Bourbon dynasty was returned to power in France.
My cat thinks he is the start of a royal dynasty that will rule the living room forever.

words.meaning: Removed from power or a high position.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: To describe how the Bourbon dynasty was removed from power during the French Revolution before being restored by the Treaty of Vienna.
hard.simple_explanation: To suddenly remove someone, like a king or leader, from their position of power.
hard.funny_explanation: It is like being the captain of the playground, but then everyone decides you are fired and makes you sit in the sandbox instead.

examples.text: The king was deposed by the people who wanted a republic instead.
The cat was deposed from the sofa when the giant dog decided it was nap time.

hard.real_world_analogy: A principal being asked to leave the school because the students took over the office.

words.meaning: Brought back to a former state or position.

medium.simple_explanation: To bring something back to its original state or position.
medium.funny_explanation: Like hitting the 'undo' button on a messy drawing or putting a dropped ice cream scoop back on the cone (though rulers are less sticky).

examples.text: The old kings were restored to their thrones after Napoleon was defeated.
I restored my phone to factory settings after it started acting like it was possessed.

words.meaning: Having control over people or a country.
Took control of another country's territory.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The author uses this to explain how France took over surrounding territories under Napoleon's rule.
hard.simple_explanation: To take control of a territory or country, usually by force, and add it to your own.
hard.funny_explanation: Imagine your neighbor builds a fence around your backyard and says, 'This is my garden now.' That is annexing!

examples.text: Germany annexed several neighboring regions during the war.
My older brother annexed my side of the bedroom just because I left for five minutes.

hard.real_world_analogy: A big corporation buying a small lemonade stand and making it part of their giant company.

words.meaning: A group of things happening in order.
The act of becoming larger or wider.

medium.simple_explanation: The act of becoming larger or taking over more territory.
medium.funny_explanation: When a country tries to 'supersize' its borders because it’s still hungry for more land.

examples.text: Neighboring states were set up to stop any future French expansion.
The expansion of my laundry pile has finally conquered the entire bedroom floor.

words.meaning: The time that has not happened yet.
The line where one country's land ends.

medium.simple_explanation: The borders or edges of a country's territory.
medium.funny_explanation: The 'Keep Out' lines on a map that tell you exactly where one country ends and the next one starts.

examples.text: Prussia gained new land on its western frontiers.
The kitchen counter is the final frontier for my dog who isn't allowed to jump up.

words.meaning: Having the power to manage or direct.
A group of states joined together.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: To describe the organization of 39 German states created by Napoleon that the Treaty of Vienna decided not to change.
hard.simple_explanation: A group of states or organizations joined together in an alliance or league.
hard.funny_explanation: It is like a 'Super-Group' of superheroes; they are all separate heroes, but they work together as one big team.

examples.text: The German confederation was a group of states that shared common goals.
The local neighborhood kids formed a confederation to protect the secret treehouse.

hard.real_world_analogy: A sports league where different teams play separately but follow the same big set of rules.

words.meaning: Not changed or affected by something.
A part or share of something.
Something that a person plans to do.
Systems where a king or queen rules.

medium.simple_explanation: Countries that are ruled by a king or queen.
medium.funny_explanation: Governments where the boss gets the job just because of who their parents were.

examples.text: European leaders wanted to restore the monarchies that Napoleon had kicked out.
In a world of monarchies, being a prince sounds cool until you realize you can't even pick your own shoes.

words.meaning: Removed from power by force.

medium.simple_explanation: Removed from power by force.
medium.funny_explanation: The ultimate 'You're Fired!' but instead of a meeting, it involves a revolution or an army.

examples.text: Many kings were overthrown during Napoleon's fast rise to power.
The king of the cafeteria was overthrown when the pizza was replaced by salad.

words.meaning: Wanting to keep traditional ways and values.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: To define the political ideology that wanted to keep traditional institutions and resisted rapid change after Napoleon's defeat.
hard.simple_explanation: Preferring traditional ways of doing things and being cautious about new changes.
hard.funny_explanation: A person who refuses to switch from a flip-phone to a smartphone because they think the old way was just fine, thank you very much!

examples.text: The conservative leaders wanted to restore the old kings back to their thrones.
My grandpa is so conservative that he still thinks the internet is a temporary fad.

hard.real_world_analogy: A chef who refuses to change a 100-year-old family recipe, even if someone suggests adding chocolate.

words.meaning: Systems of government, especially strict ones.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Refers to the specific governments or systems of rule that were established in Europe in 1815.
hard.simple_explanation: A particular government or a system or method of management.
hard.funny_explanation: Think of it as 'The Management.' When a new manager takes over the pizza shop and changes all the rules, that's a new regime.

examples.text: The new regimes in Europe were very strict about following old laws.
The new household regime involves no dessert until all broccoli is gone.

hard.real_world_analogy: A new head coach coming to a team and changing every single practice drill.

words.meaning: Having complete power without following others' wishes.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: To characterize the 1815 governments as having absolute power and not allowing any opposition.
hard.simple_explanation: Ruling with absolute power and not taking anyone else's opinion into account.
hard.funny_explanation: It's like a game of 'Simon Says' where Simon is the king and if you don't do exactly what he says, you're out forever.

examples.text: Autocratic rulers do not allow people to vote or disagree with them.
The toddler was quite autocratic, demanding that everyone wear socks on their hands.

hard.real_world_analogy: A remote control that only works for one person and has no buttons for anyone else.

words.meaning: To allow something that you do not like.
Saying what is wrong with something.

medium.simple_explanation: The act of pointing out faults or disagreeing with someone's actions.
medium.funny_explanation: When you tell the government they’re doing a bad job, and they definitely don't want to hear it.

examples.text: The new autocratic governments did not tolerate any criticism.
My brother's criticism of my singing was ignored because he has no taste.

words.meaning: Having a different opinion from the government.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: To show that the new governments in Europe would not allow people to express disagreement or protest.
hard.simple_explanation: Holding or expressing opinions that are different from those previously or officially held.
hard.funny_explanation: When the whole class wants pizza but you raise your hand and say, 'Actually, I want salad,' that's dissent!

examples.text: The government suppressed any form of dissent in the newspapers.
There was a lot of dissent in the kitchen when Dad tried to put pineapple on the pizza.

hard.real_world_analogy: Being the only person in a room full of 'Yes' people who says 'No, wait a minute!'

words.meaning: Things that are done for a purpose.

medium.simple_explanation: Actions or tasks that people do for a specific purpose.
medium.funny_explanation: Stuff people do—usually stuff the government finds suspicious, like meeting in basements to complain.

examples.text: The government tried to stop any activities that questioned their power.
My weekend activities mostly involve napping and eating snacks.

words.meaning: Tried to find or get something.

medium.simple_explanation: Tried to find or achieve something.
medium.funny_explanation: The past tense of 'seek,' as in 'they sought to be the boss,' even if nobody asked them to be.

examples.text: They sought to curb any talk of revolution.
I sought the remote control for twenty minutes before realizing I was sitting on it.

words.meaning: To control or limit something.

medium.simple_explanation: To limit, control, or hold back something.
medium.funny_explanation: Like putting a leash on a hyperactive puppy so it doesn't knock over the expensive vase of freedom.

examples.text: Kings used censorship to curb the spread of revolutionary ideas.
I need to curb my habit of buying every cool sticker I see.

words.meaning: Being legal and accepted as right.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Refers to whether a government has the legal or moral right to rule over its people.
hard.simple_explanation: The quality of being legal, fair, or acceptable according to rules or laws.
hard.funny_explanation: It's like having a 'VIP Pass' to a party. If the pass is real, you have legitimacy to be there. If it's drawn in crayon, you don't!

examples.text: People questioned the legitimacy of the king who took the throne by force.
I questioned the legitimacy of my brother's 'No Sisters Allowed' rule in the living room.

hard.real_world_analogy: A referee’s whistle: it only works because everyone agrees the referee has the right to make the calls.

words.meaning: Forced a rule or law on people.

medium.simple_explanation: Forced a rule or law on people.
medium.funny_explanation: When someone in charge says 'This is the rule now,' and you don't really get a vote in it.

examples.text: Censorship laws were imposed to control what newspapers could print.
My parents imposed a strict 'no phones at the table' law that I hate.

words.meaning: Controlling what information the public can see.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Explains how governments controlled the media to prevent the spread of revolutionary ideas.
hard.simple_explanation: The practice of examining books, movies, or news and removing parts that are considered offensive or harmful.
hard.funny_explanation: Imagine writing a letter to a friend, but your teacher blackouts all the funny words with a big marker before you can send it.

examples.text: The regime used strict censorship to stop people from reading about democracy.
My mom’s censorship of my playlist means I can only listen to nursery rhymes and bird sounds.

hard.real_world_analogy: A giant 'Bleep' sound that covers up words on TV that the station doesn't want you to hear.

words.meaning: Showed a certain idea or quality.
The state of being free from control.

medium.simple_explanation: The state of being free within society from oppressive restrictions.
medium.funny_explanation: The right to live your life without a king constantly breathing down your neck telling you what to do.

examples.text: Revolutionaries fought for the ideas of liberty and equality.
To a teenager, getting a driver's license is the ultimate symbol of liberty.

words.meaning: The right to act or speak freely.

medium.simple_explanation: The power or right to act, speak, or think as one wants.
medium.funny_explanation: The ability to do what you want, like wearing pajamas all day without a law being passed against it.

examples.text: Freedom of the press was a major demand of the liberals.
The cat finally achieved freedom when the door was left open for three seconds.

words.meaning: A person whose name is not known.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Describes the author of the 'Club of Thinkers' caricature, who hid their identity to avoid punishment.
hard.simple_explanation: Not identified by name; of unknown authorship.
hard.funny_explanation: It is like getting a secret admirer card with no name on it. Someone sent it, but they are playing 'hide and seek' with their identity.

examples.text: An anonymous artist drew the cartoon to criticize the government safely.
An anonymous person ate the last cookie, but the crumbs lead straight to the dog.

hard.real_world_analogy: A 'Mystery Guest' at a party who wears a mask so nobody knows who they really are.

words.meaning: A funny drawing that makes someone look silly.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Used to describe the satirical drawing 'The Club of Thinkers' which mocks the lack of freedom of speech.
hard.simple_explanation: A picture or description of a person in which certain striking characteristics are exaggerated for comic effect.
hard.funny_explanation: It's a drawing where someone's nose is as big as a watermelon and their ears look like elephant trunks just to make you laugh.

examples.text: The caricature made the king look like a giant, grumpy baby.
The street artist drew a caricature of me with a head the size of a balloon!

hard.real_world_analogy: A fun-house mirror that makes your head look huge and your legs look tiny.

words.meaning: Words written or carved into a surface.

medium.simple_explanation: Words that are written or carved into a surface like stone or metal.
medium.funny_explanation: Fancy writing on a wall or plaque that usually says something serious, like 'Don't touch this' or 'Kings are cool.'

examples.text: The plaque on the left side of the picture bore a strange inscription.
I found a mysterious inscription on my desk that just said 'Lunch was bad'.

words.meaning: A group of people coming together.
Given permission to do something.
A flat surface used for displaying information.
Instructions about what people must do.

medium.simple_explanation: A set of explicit regulations or principles governing conduct.
medium.funny_explanation: The 'dos and don'ts' that keep things organized, even if some of them are totally annoying.

examples.text: The club had very strict rules about staying silent.
The number one rule in my house is 'Don't eat the last cookie'.

words.meaning: A very important rule or law.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Refers to the strict 'rules' of the satirical Club of Thinkers, mocking religious or absolute laws.
hard.simple_explanation: A divine rule or a very important order that must be followed.
hard.funny_explanation: It's like a 'Mega-Rule.' Not just a regular rule, but a 'You-Must-Do-This-Or-Else' kind of rule.

examples.text: The first commandment of the club was to remain completely silent.
The cat's first commandment is: Thou shalt always trip the human on the stairs.

hard.real_world_analogy: The 'Laws of Physics'—you can't just decide to ignore gravity!

words.meaning: Having a lot of knowledge through study.

medium.simple_explanation: Having a lot of knowledge through study and experience.
medium.funny_explanation: Someone who has read so many books their brain is basically a walking library.

examples.text: The thinkers belonged to a learned society of educated men.
The learned professor couldn't figure out how to open a bag of chips.

words.meaning: People living together in a community.
A possible event that may happen.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Used in the caricature's text to describe a possible future situation that the club wants to avoid (speaking).
hard.simple_explanation: A possible event or outcome, especially one that is unpleasant.
hard.funny_explanation: A fancy word for 'just in case.' Like, 'I am bringing an umbrella for the eventuality of rain.'

examples.text: The muzzles were used to avoid the eventuality of someone speaking out.
I prepared for the eventuality of a zombie attack by buying a lot of canned beans.

hard.real_world_analogy: A 'Plan B' for something that might go wrong.

words.meaning: To stop resisting and give in.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Describes the act of giving in to the urge to talk, which the club members were forbidden from doing.
hard.simple_explanation: To stop resisting something; to give in to a pressure or temptation.
hard.funny_explanation: When you try really hard not to eat the cake, but eventually you just dive face-first into it. You succumbed!

examples.text: The thinkers were afraid they might succumb to the temptation of speech.
I tried to stay awake, but I eventually succumbed to the power of the cozy blanket.

hard.real_world_analogy: A castle gate finally breaking open after a long siege.

words.meaning: A strong desire to do something wrong.

medium.simple_explanation: A strong desire to do something, especially something you shouldn't.
medium.funny_explanation: That little voice in your head that says 'Go ahead, eat the cake' even though you're supposed to be on a diet.

examples.text: Muzzles were used to stop the temptation to speak during meetings.
The temptation to press the 'big red button' was almost too much to handle.

words.meaning: The act of talking or expressing thoughts.

medium.simple_explanation: The expression of thoughts and feelings through spoken words.
medium.funny_explanation: Blabbering, talking, or giving a formal talk—basically, using your mouth to move ideas into someone else's head.

examples.text: The members were forbidden from using free speech.
My dog’s 'speech' consists of loud barks whenever the mailman arrives.

words.meaning: Things used to stop someone from speaking.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Refers to the devices shown in the caricature that were used to physically prevent the 'thinkers' from talking.
hard.simple_explanation: Covers put over the mouth of an animal (or in this satire, a human) to prevent it from biting or speaking.
hard.funny_explanation: It's like a 'Mouth-Jail.' It keeps your words locked inside so they can't escape.

examples.text: The caricature showed philosophers wearing muzzles so they couldn't share ideas.
If I don't stop singing, my sister is going to try to put a muzzle on me.

hard.real_world_analogy: A 'Mute' button on a television, but for a person's face.

words.meaning: To show or represent in a picture.

medium.simple_explanation: To show or represent something in a drawing, painting, or story.
medium.funny_explanation: To draw a picture of something so people know what's happening without you having to explain it.

examples.text: The artist tried to depict how thinkers were being silenced.
My drawing was supposed to depict a horse, but everyone thought it was a potato with legs.

words.meaning: Belonging to the same time period.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The author uses this in the title to indicate that the history being studied is linked to the modern world we live in.
hard.simple_explanation: Belonging to or occurring in the present or the same time period.
hard.funny_explanation: It's like wearing the latest sneakers while everyone else is still stuck in the age of wooden clogs; you are living in the 'now'.

examples.text: Modern history studies the contemporary events that shaped our current world.
My grandpa thinks his flip phone is contemporary, but the rest of us are using smartphones.

hard.real_world_analogy: A live TV broadcast where the person on screen is talking to you right as they are doing the action.

words.meaning: Connected or linked to something else.
A big change in government by the people.

medium.simple_explanation: A complete and often sudden change in the way a country is governed, usually using force.
medium.funny_explanation: Imagine everyone in school suddenly deciding that students run the place and teachers have to do the homework. That’s a revolution!

examples.text: The French Revolution changed the way people thought about their rights.
I am leading a revolution against broccoli being served at dinner!

words.meaning: In spite of what was just said.
To give someone the idea or energy.
People who want more freedom and change.

medium.simple_explanation: People who believe in individual freedom and want the government to change to protect people's rights.
medium.funny_explanation: The 'let's try something new' group who thinks kings are so last season.

examples.text: The liberals wanted to make sure everyone had the right to vote.
The liberals in the cafeteria argued for more pizza and less mystery meat.

words.meaning: People wanting freedom for their specific nation.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The text describes this group as the primary critics of the conservative kings after 1815.
hard.simple_explanation: People who believe in individual freedom and the idea that people of the same culture should have their own country.
hard.funny_explanation: Imagine a group of friends who want to pick their own lunch menu (liberal) and wear matching team jerseys (nationalist).

examples.text: Liberal-nationalists across Europe protested against the lack of freedom of the press.
The liberal-nationalists of the playground demanded the right to vote on who gets the swing set first.

hard.real_world_analogy: Students in a classroom demanding they choose their own seats and form their own study groups instead of being told exactly where to sit by a strict teacher.

words.meaning: Pointed out the faults in something.
Traditional and against quick social changes.

medium.simple_explanation: A person or system that prefers to keep things exactly as they are and dislikes big changes.
medium.funny_explanation: The person who still uses a flip phone and thinks any change to the lunch menu is a disaster.

examples.text: The conservative order wanted to bring back the power of the kings.
My grandpa is very conservative; he thinks movies were better when they were silent and black-and-white.

words.meaning: The way a society is organized.

medium.simple_explanation: The way a society is organized or the current system of rules and government.
medium.funny_explanation: Not a pizza order! It's the 'Who's the Boss' chart of the entire country.

examples.text: The new conservative order tried to stop people from protesting.
When the teacher left the room, the social order broke down and flying erasers took over.

words.meaning: Controlling people by force or power.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: The book explains that the fear of being punished or silenced by the government forced many people to work in secret.
hard.simple_explanation: The act of using force to control or limit people's rights and freedoms.
hard.funny_explanation: Like a giant thumb trying to squash a bouncy spring; the harder you press, the more it wants to jump back.

examples.text: Government repression led many thinkers to form secret societies underground.

words.meaning: The act of joining parts into one unit.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: This word is used to describe the process of bringing together many small, separate states to form one large country, specifically for Germany and Italy.
hard.simple_explanation: The process of being united or made into a whole.
hard.funny_explanation: It's like taking all the random socks in your laundry basket and finally matching them into pairs so you have a complete, organized set.

examples.text: The unification of Germany was a long process led by the state of Prussia.
The unification of the two Minecraft servers meant all the players could finally build one giant castle together.

hard.real_world_analogy: Taking several small lumps of playdough and squishing them together to make one big, solid ball.

words.meaning: To bring something new into use or notice.

medium.simple_explanation: To bring something new into a place or system for the first time.
medium.funny_explanation: Like when your friend introduces you to a new song and then you play it so many times you start to hate it.

examples.text: Napoleon introduced many changes to make the government more efficient.
Let me introduce you to my new workout routine: it’s called walking to the fridge and back.

words.meaning: Relating to the management of a system.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Napoleon introduced changes to the 'administrative system' to make the government more organized, logical, and efficient.
hard.simple_explanation: Relating to the tasks of managing, organizing, and running an organization or government.
hard.funny_explanation: It's the 'boring but important' stuff—like making sure the files are in alphabetical order and everyone knows exactly whose job it is to take out the trash.

examples.text: Napoleon’s administrative reforms simplified the laws and made them the same for everyone.
My desk's administrative system is currently a disaster; I have a half-eaten apple filed under 'History Notes'.

hard.real_world_analogy: The way a school office keeps track of your attendance, grades, and lunch money so the whole school runs smoothly.

words.meaning: Working well without wasting time or energy.

medium.simple_explanation: Working in a well-organized way without wasting time or energy.
medium.funny_explanation: My method of 'cleaning' my room by shoving everything under the bed is extremely efficient.

examples.text: The new administrative system was designed to be much more efficient.
I found an efficient way to study: I put the book under my pillow and hope the knowledge travels by magic.

words.meaning: Land areas that are under one government's rule.

medium.simple_explanation: An area of land that is under the control of a specific ruler or country.
medium.funny_explanation: My bed and the space around the TV are my strictly guarded territories where no one is allowed.

examples.text: Napoleon ruled over many different territories across Europe.
The cat believes that all cardboard boxes in this house are its personal, sovereign territories.
